sections.heading: Enhanced piezoelectric energy harvester performance using magnetic force and thermal energy
sections.text:
Almuatasim Alomari, Ashok Batra, Arjun Tan, and Marius Schamschula

Department of Physics, Chemistry, and Mathematics, Alabama A&M University, Huntsville, AL, USA

sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text: One possible approach of improving the performance of energy harvesters is to use energy harvester with an external magnetic force to create a nonlinear coupling system. In this work, we report experimental results of a single' piezoelectric cantilever beam (PCB) with tip mass or conventional piezoelectric energy harvester (CPEH), and the effect of applying an external magnetic force. The output voltage and power at optimal resistance was $7 . 6 2 \lor$ and $0 . 6 2 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { W } ,$ respectively, at the resonance frequency of approximately 11 Hz of a CPEH. Also, the output voltage and average power at optimal resistance was $8 . 5 6 ~ \mathsf { V }$ and $0 . 4 4 ~ \mathrm { m W } ,$ respectively, at resonance frequency of $7 H z$ of a PCB with fixed opposing magnet. Furthermore, the output voltage and average power at optimal resistance was 13.31 V and $1 . 7 7 \ : \mathrm { m W } ,$ respectively, at resonance frequency of 11 Hz of a PCB with opposing magnet attached at a second cantilever. In addition, comparison between the experimental results of all different configurations showed a reasonable enhancement of performance of energy harvester when an external magnetic force added over the main PCB. Finally, the performance of a multisource energy harvester with magnetic, thermal and mechanical sources is also presented in this study. In this case, it is demonstrated that increase in output voltage with temperature gradient under effect of magnetic force; the results of $2 ^ { \mathsf { n d } }$ and $3 ^ { \mathrm { r d } }$ model showed $4 4 \%$ and $9 9 \%$ enhancement of its original output voltage value at $1 . 2 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ and $2 . 7 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C$ temperature difference, respectively.

sections.heading: KEYWORDS
sections.text: Energy harvesting; piezoelectric; magnetic force; thermal energy; vibration

sections.heading: .Introduction
sections.text:
Harvesting energy from ambient mechanical vibrations has been suggested as a promising technique to deliver power in conditions where battery-operated is impractical or difficult. Vibration energy harvesting from ambient environment could be useful in various low-power electronic applications such as, Radiofrequency identification (RFID) and wireless sensor networks (WSNs) [1,2]. The most popular vibration energy harvesting technique is to capture power from the electrostatic [3-7], electromagnetic [8-12], piezoelectric [13-16], and magnetostrictive [17-20] vibration energy harvesters (VEHs). The most current VEH devices are based on cantilever beam structure which generates continues or intermittent resonance frequency tuning. The typical piezoelectric cantilever beam (PCB) can produce maximum power when its resonance frequency matches the frequency of the vibration source [21]. However, researchers proof that the resonance frequency of PCB can be changed or improved by using different approaches such as, changing geometrical PCB structure [22, 23], adding dynamic magnifier [24-27], using energy harvesting cantilever arrays [28-30], and using external magnetic forces [21, 31-36]. To date, there are a good research interests that have attempted to capture the power from passive tuning of magnetic coupling of piezoelectric cantilever beam [21, 32-36]. For example, applying magnetic force acting above the PCB decreases the spring constant and the resonance frequency of the PCB [21, 31], although an attractive force acting along the axis of the PCB applies axial tension, and increases the resonance frequency [37].

In the present article, we aim to harvest electrical energy using the effect of magnetic force and thermal energy on magnetic tip mass of PCB under different configurations. Furthermore, objective is to find out the effect of distance between a fixed or movable magnet and magnet at the tip of cantilever on harvested power. Here, we focus on the commonly employed 31-mode of harvesting from bending induced by vibrations. The performance of the piezoelectric energy harvesting device based on PCB was evaluated and demonstrated via experiments thereby proving the concept of improving the performance of our energy harvester via a commercial materials system.

sections.heading: 2. Experimental conception and technique
sections.text:
The conventional piezoelectric energy harvester (CPEH) system is based on a single PCB with a mass connected to its tip. The CPEH harvests power around single resonance frequency and shows linear oscillations under cantilever motion. Therefore, adding extra magnetic force on PEH may expand the frequency bandwidth and increase the harvested power of harvester and shows nonlinear behavior. The configurations of piezoelectric cantilevered beam (PCB) utilizing a magnetic force are shown in Figure 1. The cantilever is manufactured using commercially available unimorph PCB composed of M8528-P2 element made by Smart Material Corp., Sarasota (FL) USA. The piezoelectric element made of PZT material extends $8 5 \mathrm { m m }$ along the total cantilever length of $1 0 3 \mathrm { m m }$ , and the remainder is fiber only. The experimental setup is shown in Figure 2. Energy harvesting measurements were carried out initially by attaching a tip mass (magnets) at the front of the PCB. Secondly, the opposing magnets of the same type is attached directly to the magnets holder. Finally, upper beam with a tip mass (magnet) has identical and tuned resonance frequency of main PCB was connected to fixed base over the main PCB. The experimental set-up consists a small-mechanical shaker (Bruel and Kjaer Model Type 4810) and function generator (Agilent/Keysight 33500B) to produce a range of vibration frequencies and a high-power amplifier (Bruel and Kjaer Model 2718) to create a cyclic force of the required magnitude and frequency. A multimeter (Keithley Model 2110) measured the output voltage from the harvester and a variable impedance module. Data acquisition was achieved via a Picoscope (Pico-Technology Model 4224). To avoid any interference from the noise in the surrounding environment, all experiments were performed on an isolated optical bench. Table 1. When the piezoelectric harvester is subjected to vibrations by the experimental setup it produces an AC electrical output and the output signal from the harvester is connected to a variable resistive load or an AC-DC circuit with a capacitive load. In all measurements, the shaker acceleration is set to approximately $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m } / \mathsf { s } ^ { 2 }$ close from gravitational acceleration, and the frequency swept from 0 to $2 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ in $1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ steps. The opposing magnets placed at specific distance of the PCB supplies a maximum output voltage and a symmetrical balance of the cantilever during vibration. The horizontal and vertical separation between the magnets (designated by $d _ { I }$ and $d _ { 2 }$ , respectively) provide the best compensation for the spring force, and makes the effective restoring force as small as possible near the equilibrium point [21].

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In conclusion, we report experimental results of a single piezoelectric cantilever beam (PCB) with tip mass or conventional piezoelectric energy harvester (CPEH) and the effect of adding external magnetic force using fixed and movable opposing magnet. The output voltage and power at optimal resistance was $7 . 6 2 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and $0 . 6 2 \ \mathrm { m W } ,$ respectively, at the resonance frequency of approximately $1 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ of a CPEH. Also, the output voltage and average power at optimal resistance was $8 . 5 6 \mathrm { V }$ and $0 . 4 4 ~ \mathrm { m W } ,$ respectively, at resonance frequency of $7 \ \mathrm { H z }$ of a PCB with fixed opposing magnet. Furthermore, the output voltage and average power at optimal resistance was $1 3 . 3 1 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and $1 . 7 7 \mathrm { m W } ,$ respectively, at resonance frequency of $1 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ of a PCB with opposing magnet attached at a second cantilever. In short, comparisons between the experimental results of all different configurations showed a good enhancement of energy harvester when an external magnetic force added over the main PCB. The output power was increased from $0 . 6 2 \mathrm { m W }$ to $1 . 7 7 \mathrm { m W }$ at resonance frequency of $1 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ showing $1 8 5 \%$ enhanced when opposing magnet attached at a second cantilever over main PCB. Finally, the performance of a multisource energy harvester with thermal, magnetic and mechanical sources is presented. In this case, it is demonstrated that increasing in output voltage with temperature gradient under the presence of magnetic force; the maximum output voltage of $2 ^ { \mathrm { n d } }$ model at a frequency value of $6 \mathrm { H z }$ and an optimum resistance of $9 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ was observed to increase from 3.74 to $5 . 3 7 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ under temperature difference of $1 . 2 \ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ showing about $4 4 \%$ enhancement. On the other hand, the maximum output voltage of $3 ^ { \mathrm { r d } }$ model at a frequency value of $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and an optimum resistance of $9 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ was increased from 2.37 to $4 . 7 2 \mathrm { V }$ under temperature difference of $2 . 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ showing about $9 9 \%$ enhancement of its original value.
